extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and stating patent rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103 and 112 (form paragraphs, legal tests, and procedural requirements) in office actions. Focuses on when and how to apply particular statutory grounds and supporting explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying 35 U.S.C. 102(e) for references with earlier filing dates
rubrics_metrics.description: This paragraph is used to reject over a reference (patent or published application) with an earlier filing date that discloses the claimed invention, and that only qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e). The reference must have either a common assignee or at least one common inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do NOT use this form paragraph if the reference qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or (b) (use form paragraph 7.21 instead). Do not use when the reference is disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) as prior art in a 103(a) rejection. See Examiner Notes for form paragraph 7.12 to determine the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date of the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIPA / pre-AIPA date determinations for 35 U.S.C. 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as amended by the American Inventors Protection Act (AIPA) must be applied if the reference is either (a) filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a), or (b) a WIPO publication of an international application with an international filing date on or after November 29, 2000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-AIPA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) must be applied if the reference is a U.S. patent issued directly or indirectly from an international application filed prior to November 29, 2000. See Examiner Notes for form paragraphs 7.12 and 7.12.01 for assistance in determining the 102(e) date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) over reference with common assignee/inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over a reference that has a common assignee or at least one common inventor and which constitutes prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the obviousness (insert explanation in bracket 4). The rejection might be overcome by: (1) a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed in the reference was derived from the inventor of this application (not an invention 'by another'); or (2) a showing of a date of invention for the claimed subject matter corresponding to the subject matter disclosed but not claimed in the reference. Provide full explanation applying the Graham v. Deere factors where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a 'further in view of' combination rejection (35 U.S.C. 103(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over [reference A] as applied to claim [X], and further in view of [reference B].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 7.22 must be preceded by form paragraph 7.21. An explanation applying the Graham v. Deere test must follow this form paragraph. If relying on 102(e) prior art dates, use AIPA/pre-AIPA rules as applicable (see notes for 7.12/7.12.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham v. Deere factual inquiries for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co. that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a): 1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art. 2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue. 3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art. 4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form paragraph may be used, if appropriate, in response to an argument of the use of Graham v. Deere. An explanation of the Graham analysis must follow form paragraph 7.22 or similar rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use combined 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103(a) rejection (form paragraph 7.27)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102([x]) as anticipated by or, in the alternative, under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over [reference].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph is NOT intended to be commonly used as a substitute for a single 102 or 103 rejection. Use only when appropriate, e.g.: (a) claim interpretation dispute where one interpretation yields 102 and another yields 103; (b) reference discloses all claim limitations except a property or function and examiner cannot determine whether the property is inherent; (c) genus/species disclosure issues; (d) product-by-process same product produced by different process; (e) means-plus-function uncertainties; (f) overlapping ranges where no specific example exists. Provide a full explanation following the form paragraph and precede with form paragraphs 7.07, 7.08-7.14 as appropriate, and 7.20 or 7.103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability and requirements of 35 U.S.C. 103(b) for biotechnological processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding subsection (a), a biotechnological process using or resulting in a composition of matter that is novel under section 102 and nonobvious under subsection (a) shall be considered nonobvious if certain conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 103(b) requires: (A) claims to the process and the composition of matter be in the same application or in separate applications having the same effective filing date; (B) both be owned or subject to assignment to the same person at time of invention; (C) a patent on the process also contain claims to the composition, or if composition claimed in another patent, the patents expire on the same date; (D) process falls within statutory definition (e.g., genetically altering organisms, cell fusion procedures, methods of using product); (E) a timely election to proceed under 103(b) by petition under 37 CFR 1.182. Provide petition showing all requirements satisfied; timeliness rules and special handling (issue fee/appeal brief dates, reissue in case of error) are described in guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary focus on prior art; limit undue emphasis on non-prior-art rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary object of examination is to determine whether claims are patentable over the prior art. This consideration should not be relegated while undue emphasis is given to nonprior art or 'technical' rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate effort on truly essential matters and minimize effort on technical rejections which are not critical. Where a major technical (non-prior-art) rejection is proper (e.g., lack of proper disclosure, undue breadth, utility), state it with a full development of the reasons rather than a mere conclusion with stereotyped language. Use appropriate MPEP sections for nonstatutory subject matter, double patenting, new matter, foreign filing without license, disclaimers, reissue, etc. Incorporating form paragraph language reduces misunderstanding as to grounds of rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 (statutory classes and nonpatentable examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentable subject matter is limited to 'any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof.' Certain things are examples of nonstatutory subject matter (printed matter, a naturally occurring article substantially unaltered, scientific principles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite MPEP § 2105 for microorganisms and § 2106-2106.02 for algorithms/computer programs. Use form paragraphs 7.04-7.05.03 to reject under 35 U.S.C. 101; paragraph 7.04 (statute quotation) must precede first use of 101 in first actions on the merits and final rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement under 35 U.S.C. 101
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection on the ground of lack of utility includes inoperativeness (e.g., perpetual motion). A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 for lack of utility should not be based on grounds that the invention is frivolous, fraudulent, or against public policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the lack of utility (see Juicy Whip Inc. v. Orange Bang Inc. precedent). Use MPEP § 2107 for guidelines governing utility rejections and § 2107.01-2107.03 for legal precedent. Use the form paragraph 7.05 (heading only) followed by the specific 7.05.01-7.05.03 paragraphs as appropriate; 7.04 must precede 7.05 in first actions and final rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatted utility/enablement rejection combining 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112 (first paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is not supported by either a [asserted utility] or a well-established utility; and claim also rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph for lack of enablement if the specification would not enable one skilled in the art to make/use the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Format A, B, or C as appropriate: Format A inserts 'specific and substantial' where appropriate; Format B inserts 'credible'; Format C addresses multiple utilities that are not specific/substantial/credible. When specification is not enabling, make a separate enablement rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 applying In re Wands factors and undue experimentation analysis (MPEP §§ 2164-2164.08(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Atomic Energy Act limitations on patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: No patent shall be granted for any invention useful solely in the utilization of special nuclear material or atomic energy in an atomic weapon (42 U.S.C. 2181(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms 'atomic energy' and 'special nuclear material' are defined in the Act. Sections 151(c)/(d) set categories of pending applications relating to atomic energy that must be reported to the Department of Energy. Applications are screened under 37 CFR 1.14(d); rejections based on the Atomic Energy Act must be made only by TC work group 3640 personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph — written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, as failing to comply with the written description requirement: the claim contains subject matter not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to one skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. In the office action identify the subject matter not properly described by suitable reference to pages/lines/figures and explain your position, including any unresolved examiner questions that raise doubt as to possession at time of filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph — enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, as failing to comply with the enablement requirement: the claim contains subject matter not described in the specification in such a way as to enable one skilled in the art to make and/or use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede this rejection with form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. Identify claimed subject matter not enabled and explain why the specification is not enabling by applying the In re Wands factors (858 F.2d 731) and related MPEP sections. Explain any unresolved examiner questions that raise doubt as to enablement. If the problem concerns scope, use form paragraph 7.31.03 instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph — scope of enablement (commensurateness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, because the specification, while being enabling for some embodiments, does not reasonably provide enablement for other claimed subject matter; i.e., the claims are not commensurate in scope with the enabling disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. Identify what the specification does enable (by reference) and the aspects of the claims not enabled. State whether the specification fails to enable one to 'make', 'use', or 'make and use' the invention commensurate with claim scope. Apply In re Wands factors and include explanations of unresolved examiner questions where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph — best mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, because the best mode contemplated by the inventor has not been disclosed; evidence of concealment of the best mode is to be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. In bracket show basis for holding best mode has been concealed (e.g., poor quality of disclosure). Use of this form paragraph should be rare; see MPEP §§ 2165-2165.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph — essential subject matter missing from claims (enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph when subject matter considered critical or essential to practice of the invention is missing from the claim(s) and therefore not enabled by the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. Recite omitted subject matter in the office action; cite statement/argument/date/drawing or other evidence showing applicant considered the feature essential. Give rationale for considering the omitted subject matter critical/essential. Use form paragraph 7.33.01 when an essential component or step is not recited in the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph — claims must 'particularly point out and distinctly claim' (indefiniteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention; failure to do so supports a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.30.02 (statutory quotation) in first actions and final rejections. Rejections under 112, second paragraph should be supported by one or more specific form paragraphs (7.34.02 - 7.34.11 etc.), and identify particular terms or limitations rendering the claim indefinite where possible. If none of the form paragraphs fit, provide a full explanation of the deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology used inconsistent with accepted meaning (claim indefiniteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where applicant acts as own lexicographer to redefine a term contrary to its ordinary meaning, the written description must clearly redefine the claim term and set forth the uncommon definition to put one reasonably skilled in the art on notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.34.02 following 7.34.01. Identify the term, its meaning as used in the claim, and the accepted meaning. Provide support for the accepted meaning via references (textbook/dictionary). This paragraph should only be used where the specification does not clearly redefine the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative term / term of degree rendering claim indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: A relative term used in a claim that is not defined by the claim or by the specification, and for which the specification provides no standard for ascertaining the requisite degree, renders the claim indefinite because one of ordinary skill would not be reasonably apprised of the scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.34.03 after 7.34.01. Explain which parameter, quantity, or limitation in the claim is rendered indefinite by the relative/degree term. Identify how the lack of standard prevents ascertainment of scope.
